content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding the CAP Theorem and PACELC Theorem in Database Design"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When designing distributed database systems, architects must navigate fundamental trade-offs regarding data consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. The CAP theorem and its extension, the PACELC theorem, provide the theoretical framework for understanding these trade-offs."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The CAP Theorem"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Formulated by Eric Brewer, the CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of the following three guarantees:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Consistency (C): Every read receives the most recent write or an error."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Availability (A): Every non-failing request receives a non-error response, without the guarantee that it contains the most recent write."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Partition Tolerance (P): The system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed by the network between nodes."},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"In distributed systems, network partitions (P) are a physical inevitability. Therefore, architects essentially choose between Consistency and Availability during a partition event, leading to CP or AP systems."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"The Limitation of CAP"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"While CAP is useful, it only describes system behavior during a network partition. It says nothing about the system's behavior when the network is running normally (without partitions). To address this, Daniel Abadi formulated the PACELC theorem."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"The PACELC Theorem"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The PACELC theorem states that: If there is a Partition (P), how does the system trade off Availability and Consistency (A and C); Else (E), when the system is running normally without partitions, how does the system trade off Latency and Consistency (L and C)?"},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"PACELC Structure: IF Partition -> Choose(A, C) ELSE -> Choose(L, C)"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Database Classifications using PACELC"},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PC/EC (e.g., Google Spanner, HBase): Favors consistency during partitions and prioritizes consistency over latency during normal operations."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PA/EL (e.g., DynamoDB, Cassandra): Favors availability during partitions and prioritizes low latency over strict consistency during normal operations."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PA/EC (e.g., MongoDB default): Favors availability during partitions, but chooses consistency over latency during normal operations by routing reads/writes through a primary node."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"When designing modern database architectures, relying solely on CAP is insufficient. Utilizing the PACELC theorem allows engineers to evaluate both failure-mode behaviors and normal-operation performance trade-offs effectively."}]
